subject: Communication
title: Sunk Cost and Commitment Traps
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Sunk Cost and Commitment Traps.

hook.text: You've watched 90 minutes of a terrible movie. You stay because you already 'invested' the time.

buildup.text: The sunk cost fallacy: we continue behaviors because of past investment, not future benefit.

discovery.text: Manipulators exploit this by getting you invested early — time, money, or emotion — then escalating demands.

twist.text: Casinos, abusive relationships, and bad business deals all trap people through accumulated sunk costs.

climax.text: The rational move is always to evaluate future costs and benefits — ignoring what you've already spent.

punchline.text: What you've spent is gone. Only what's ahead matters.

quiz.question: What is the sunk cost fallacy?
options: Continuing because of past investment, not future benefit

details.summary: The sunk cost fallacy keeps us investing in failing projects because we have already spent money, time, or effort. Commitment escalation makes us double down rather than cut losses. This trap affects personal relationships, business ventures, and government policy alike.
details.whyItMatters: Sunk cost thinking wastes resources on doomed endeavors. Learning to evaluate future value independent of past investment is a critical life skill.
takeaways: Past investment should not influence future decisions
Commitment escalation makes us double down on mistakes
Walk-away decisions improve with awareness of this bias

faq.question: Why is it so hard to abandon sunk costs?
faq.answer: Abandoning a sunk cost feels like admitting failure and wasting everything invested. Loss aversion makes the pain of walking away feel greater than the potential gain. Social pressure adds weight since others may judge the decision to quit as weakness.

faq.question: How can organizations avoid commitment traps?
faq.answer: Set predefined kill criteria before starting projects. Use independent reviewers who are not emotionally invested. Regularly ask whether you would start this project today knowing what you know now. Companies like Intel have formal exit processes to overcome escalation.
